articleHeadline: 50 years after the identification of Ebola: the healthcare challenge of facing all its variants.
articleSummary: Bundibugyo outbreak of 2026 tests Ebola response models that historically focused on a single species. Five decades after Ebola virus identification, four human-pathogenic species in the Orthoebolavirus genus—Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, and Tai Forest—drive regional risk; Reston and Bombali have not caused human disease. The Zaire-centric approach has yielded vaccines, monoclonal antibody cocktails, and diagnostic assays, but these were developed against Zaire’s glycoprotein and validated on Zaire genomes, with cross-species protection assumed rather than measured. Bundibugyo’s sequence divergence shows that Zaire-based tests lose sensitivity, risking false negatives and undercounting non-Zaire infections. A comprehensive response requires pan-ebolavirus diagnostics plus species-specific tests, multivalent or mosaic vaccines and conserved T-cell epitope–based therapeutics, and rapid updates as antigenic data change. Continuous genomic surveillance and sustained operational readiness—beyond inventory—including simulation training and VR modules are essential to accelerate diagnosis, vaccine/therapy development, and outbreak response for future pathogens.

Humans contract via infected fleas, direct contact with infected animals or their tissues, or inhalation of droplets; pets can bring infected fleas indoors. The 'blocked flea' mechanism—biofilm buildup in a flea gut causes starvation and repeated biting—drives transmission. Globally, plague exists on all continents except Australia and Antarctica; WHO reports about 551 suspected and 378 confirmed cases annually, mostly from Africa (DR Congo, Madagascar). The last large outbreak was Madagascar in 2017 with 2,348 cases. In the U.S., about five human cases per year, all in the West: states west of the 100th meridian (e.g., MT, WY, CO, NM, AZ, CA, OR, WA, NV, ID, UT, TX, ND, SD, NE, KS, OK). No vaccine in the U.S.; early antibiotics are effective. Prevention: avoid handling wildlife, fleas, and keep pets from beds.

articleHeadline: Andrographolide from Andrographis paniculata as a potential inhibitor of the novel malarial drug target PF11_0189: a comprehensive in silico approach
articleSummary: Global malaria deaths exceed 600,000 annually, with partial artemisinin resistance spreading across South and Southeast Asia, creating urgency for antimalarials with new mechanisms. PF11_0189, an essential Plasmodium falciparum M16 insulinase-family metallopeptidase lacking significant human homologs, is a pharmacologically underexploited target. Using ethnopharmacology from Northeast India—where Andrographis paniculata (Kalmegh) is repeatedly documented as antimalarial—the study deployed a multi-layered in silico pipeline to identify PF11_0189 inhibitors. Docking ten phytochemicals against decoys yielded andrographolide as the top hit (ROC-AUC 0.81; EF@1% 12.4; docking energy -8.4 kcal/mol, better than chloroquine at -6.9). Andrographolide shows a clean drug-likeness profile (zero Lipinski violations; non-HERG; non-P-gp substrate; PAINS/Brenk-negative) and, in three 100-ns MD runs, forms a stable complex (backbone RMSD < 2.5 Å) with binding energy -42.3 kJ/mol, anchored by five hotspot residues: Glu-203, Thr-89, Phe-116, Trp-214, Ser-112. This purely computational work, using an AlphaFold2 receptor, designates andrographolide as a prioritized, testable PF11_0189 inhibitor; wet-lab validation is still required.

articleHeadline: Ferritin Ratios Fail to Outperform Routine Blood Tests in Adult Dengue
articleSummary: In a prospective study at SMIMER Hospital, Surat, India (June 2020–November 2021), 100 adults with WHO 2009‑confirmed dengue were evaluated to test ferritin kinetics and composite ferritin-derived ratios against routine tests for predicting severe outcomes. articleHeadline: Taipei Reports Imported Dengue Fever Cases: Taiwan Records Infections After Vietnam Trip.
articleSummary: Two imported dengue fever cases linked to a Phu Quoc, Vietnam trip were confirmed in Taiwan, alongside a new local case in Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City. The imported cases involve a man and a woman from Taichung, aged 40–60, who traveled in late October for eight days; after returning they developed fever, headaches, and muscle pain and were diagnosed by physicians. The local case is a woman in her 40s, with the infection source under investigation. Health authorities mapped exposure and residence for a 13-person travel group; eight others live in Taichung, two in Nantou, and one in New Taipei City. Monitoring extends through December 6, with vector control and breeding-site removal at residences. Taiwan has 245 confirmed cases this year, including 18 local transmissions and 227 imported, with exposures mainly in Southeast and South Asia (notably Vietnam and Bangladesh). Travelers should use protective clothing and insect repellent; seek care for fever or rash after return and report travel history; residents should remove standing water.

articleHeadline: High Case Numbers in Asia and the Americas: How Travelers Protect Themselves from Dengue
articleSummary: Dengue cases surge in Asia and the Americas, with Bangladesh reporting about 136,930 cases and 427 deaths this year, and end-Oct hospitalizations reaching nearly 2,000 in a single day. Vietnam records ~131,205 cases, ~37% higher than last year, concentrated in the southern Ho Chi Minh City metro area (~42,500). In Latin America, Honduras exceeds 12,000 cases by end-Oct; Mexico, Bolivia, Peru, and Colombia show up to 53% increases over the prior four weeks; the Dominican Republic has 415 cases by week 40, notably in La Altagracia, La Romana and Puerto Plata. Dengue is transmitted by daytime-biting Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus in urban settings; incubation is 4–10 days. Re-infection with a different serotype raises risk of severe disease. Prevention emphasizes long clothing, effective repellents, and bed nets. Vaccination: Stiko caps use behind prior lab-confirmed infection; BCRT/CRM advocate Qdenga even without prior infection; EU-approved for ages 4+ with two doses at least three months apart.
